notes.meaning: Ezekiel's heavenly guide leads him back to the outer gate that faces east. The prophet had finished viewing the measurements of the temple courtyards, but now he is brought to this main entrance. This was the exact gate where the vision of God's presence had departed years earlier, and it was now set to receive Him back.

Ezekiel sees the radiant glory of the God of Israel arriving from the east, lighting up the whole land. The sound of His voice is like the roar of rushing waters, displaying His supreme power and majesty. God had departed toward the east when Jerusalem was judged, and now He returns to dwell with His people again.

The glorious sight was just like the vision Ezekiel saw when God first called him by the Kebar River, and when he was sent to announce Jerusalem's destruction. The prophet speaks of himself as destroying the city because he had pronounced God's sure word of judgment against it. Overwhelmed by the holiness and majesty of the Lord, Ezekiel falls facedown in humble worship.

The bright glory of the Lord enters the temple through the gate facing east. The sins of Israel had once driven God's presence away from the old sanctuary, but now His presence comes to fill this new house. His return shows that God has restored His favor and fellowship to His repentant people.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teaching links this verse to the walled-up Eastern Gate in Jerusalem today, or to Jesus' entry into the city. Others point out that this is not the gate Jesus used.

notes.meaning: The Holy Spirit lifts Ezekiel up and brings him into the inner courtyard. From there, Ezekiel sees that the glory of the Lord has completely filled the temple building, just as it once filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. God's presence transforms the newly measured structure into a living home for worship.

While the guide who measured the buildings stands beside Ezekiel, God speaks directly to the prophet from inside the temple. Having this heavenly companion standing by strengthens Ezekiel as he hears the voice of the Almighty. Believers can listen with confidence knowing God provides help whenever He speaks His word.

The Lord declares that this temple is the place of His throne and where His feet rest, promising to live among His people forever. He announces that Israel and their kings will never again dishonor His holy name through idolatry or by placing royal tombs near His house. God demands complete devotion because He alone is Israel's true King.

differ.view: The temple and throne refer to a literal future reign of Christ on earth during a thousand-year kingdom.
The vision uses earthly temple language to picture Christ dwelling spiritually in His church and in the new creation.

notes.meaning: God reminds Ezekiel how earlier kings built their own palaces and idol altars right next to His sanctuary, with only a thin wall separating them. By setting their corrupt worship next to God's house, they insulted His holy majesty. This blatant disrespect was the reason God consumed the nation in His righteous anger.

The Lord commands the people to remove all idolatry and keep royal burial monuments far away from His sanctuary. True worship requires putting away anything that treats human rulers as rivals to the living God. When the people remove these defilements, God promises to remain in their midst forever.

God tells Ezekiel to describe the temple and its design to the exiled people so they will reflect on their sins and feel ashamed. Looking closely at God's holy and orderly plan was meant to show them how far they had wandered from His standards. Seeing God's goodness and holiness leads people to genuine repentance.

If the people truly repent and show shame over their past sins, Ezekiel is to teach them every detail of the temple's rules, gates, and arrangement. He must write these plans down clearly so they can study them and obey them faithfully. God entrusts deeper understanding of His ways to hearts that are humble and sorrowful over sin.

The basic rule for the new temple is that the entire top of the mountain around it must be treated as most holy. In earlier times, only the innermost room of the temple carried this level of holiness, but now the whole sacred grounds share in it. God's dwelling place requires complete purity and reverence in every corner.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read Ezekiel 38–48 as an early kind of vision writing about an ideal world, given to the exiles. On this view it cares more about ordering holy space than about real buildings.

notes.meaning: A new section opens with the measurements of the great altar for burnt offerings, the center of worship. The measurements use the long cubit, which was an ordinary forearm length plus a handbreadth (about three inches longer than normal). A base gutter and raised border ran around the bottom to catch and drain sacrificial blood and ashes.

The altar was built in layered tiers, getting narrower as it rose from the ground. The first tier rose two cubits high with a walking ledge one cubit wide, and the next section rose four cubits higher with another ledge. These stepped ledges gave the priests a stable platform to walk around the altar while attending to the fire and offerings.

The top hearth of the altar rose another four cubits, with four horn-like points projecting upward from its corners. These horns symbolized strength and divine protection, and sacrificial animals were sometimes tied to them. The elevated hearth lifted the offerings high toward heaven like a small mountain dedicated to God.

The top surface of the altar hearth formed a perfect square, measuring twelve cubits on each side. A square shape in scripture represents balance, order, and stability in God's sacred arrangements. Its generous size provided plenty of space for the wood and the sacrifices that would be offered on it.

The upper ledge was also square, measuring fourteen cubits on each side, with a small rim and a gutter running around it. The steps leading up to the altar faced east, meaning the priests faced west toward the temple as they climbed. This design kept the priests from facing east, guarding them against pagan customs of bowing to the rising sun.

The Lord provides instructions for dedicating the altar on the day it is constructed, before regular worship begins. Sacrifices and the sprinkling of blood were required to cleanse the altar and prepare it for holy service. In God's order, the altar itself had to be consecrated before it could be used for the people's gifts.

differ.view: This temple will be built during Christ's thousand-year reign. Its sacrifices will not forgive sin, since Christ did that once for all. They will be memorials or object lessons about sin.
The temple was never meant to be built. Its measurements are symbolic, and its worship points to Christ and the new creation.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel is told to provide a young bull as a sin offering to the priests from the family of Zadok. Zadok's line was chosen because their ancestors stayed loyal to the Lord when others fell into idolatry. The sin offering made atonement, a cleansing act that wiped away ritual impurity so the priests could safely serve in God's presence.

differ.view: These future animal sacrifices during the millennium will serve as memorials looking back to Christ's death, without taking away sins.
These sacrifices are Old Testament figures pointing forward to the once-for-all sacrifice of Jesus Christ, rather than literal future offerings.

notes.meaning: The priest was to smear some of the bull's blood on the four horns of the altar, the corners of its upper ledge, and the rim around it. Applying blood to its outer edges purified the altar and set it apart for God. This ritual reminded everyone that drawing near to a holy God requires purification from sin.

After using its blood on the altar, the priest had to take the rest of the bull outside the inner sanctuary and burn it completely in an assigned place. The priests could not eat this offering because it carried away the ritual impurity of the altar's consecration. Disposing of the body outside the holy area preserved the pure condition of the temple courts.

On the second day, the priests were to sacrifice a flawless male goat as a sin offering. The altar was to be cleansed with its blood in the exact same way as on the first day with the bull. This continued cleansing taught that setting apart a place for God takes thorough and patient preparation.

Once the sin offering on the second day was complete, the priests were to bring an unblemished young bull and a flawless ram. These animals were dedicated as burnt offerings, representing total surrender and devotion to God. Bringing animals without defect showed that the Lord deserves only the finest gifts His people can offer.

The priests were to bring the bull and ram before the Lord and throw salt generously over them before burning them on the altar. In the ancient world, salt stood for preservation, permanence, and the lasting bond of God's covenant. The animals were then completely consumed by fire as a sweet-smelling offering dedicated to the Lord.

For seven straight days, the priests were to offer a daily goat for a sin offering, alongside a young bull and a ram for burnt offerings. This eight-day cleansing pattern matched the historic dedications of the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. Repeating these rituals showed how completely the altar had to be prepared before regular worship could begin.

Through these seven days of offerings, the priests made atonement for the altar and consecrated it for God's use. The Hebrew phrase for consecration literally means filling the hands, picturing an altar continually supplied and busy with sacred gifts. Only after this thorough purification was the altar ready for its ongoing ministry.

From the eighth day onward, the altar was fully consecrated, allowing the priests to offer the people's regular burnt offerings and peace offerings. Once the altar was made holy, the Lord promised that He would gladly accept the people and their gifts. True sacrifice and proper cleansing reopen the way to full and joyful fellowship with God.
